title: Why the Gulf states won't side with America
gist: Two INSS researchers argue that Operation Epic Fury was a tactical success and a strategic failure: Iran absorbed heavy damage but retained the coercive capabilities that matter — the ability to threaten Hormuz shipping, energy infrastructure and proxy networks — and has institutionalised that leverage via a new Persian Gulf Strait Association that would collect tolls from commercial vessels. Because Washington cannot shield their infrastructure, the Gulf monarchies are accelerating toward multi-alignment: keeping US security ties while covertly rebuilding relations with Tehran and deepening engagement with China.

insights.claim: The Washington-Tehran Memorandum of Understanding signed on 17 June collapsed after Iran continued targeting commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz, triggering tit-for-tat US airstrikes including attacks on Bahrain and Kuwait, both of which host US bases.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: The negotiated pause lasted under a month and broke on shipping attacks — treat Hormuz interdiction, not nuclear talks, as the escalation trigger to monitor.
insights.locator: The initial trigger for the collapse of the MoU

insights.claim: An Iranian drone strike on a US-owned gas storage vessel at Egypt's Port of Damietta and missile attacks on US forces in Jordan prompted American retaliatory airstrikes, while renewed Houthi threats to blockade the Bab al-Mandeb Strait raised concerns over Suez Canal transit for Gulf oil and LNG.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Risk is now spread across two chokepoints simultaneously — Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb — which compounds tanker rates, war-risk premia and European LNG routing costs.

insights.claim: Iran launched coordinated missile and drone strikes against American installations and critical infrastructure across the Gulf, killing three American service members at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on 17 July.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: US casualties raise the domestic political cost of restraint and the odds of a broader American campaign — an escalation marker for oil risk premia.
insights.locator: The escalation between Washington and Tehran reached its apogee

insights.claim: Trump announced the United States would reinstate a naval blockade preventing ships from entering or leaving Iranian ports, and claimed Washington would be 'reimbursed' at a rate of 20 per cent for securing safe passage for commercial cargo vessels transiting the Gulf, a proposal he subsequently reversed.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: A proposed 20 per cent US transit toll on Gulf shipping — announced and then reversed — signals policy improvisation that shippers and insurers cannot underwrite against.
insights.quote: Trump additionally claimed that Washington would be ‘reimbursed’ at a rate of 20 per cent for securing safe passage for commercial cargo vessels transiting the Gulf

insights.claim: Trump postponed a significant wave of retaliatory strikes against Iran to allow more time for diplomacy, maintaining a dual-track strategy of military pressure and negotiation even as violence escalated, with indirect talks continuing via Qatari and Pakistani mediation.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Qatar and Pakistan are the live mediation channels — announcements from Doha or Islamabad are the leading indicators of de-escalation.

insights.claim: Iran's asymmetric strategy does not require permanently closing the Strait of Hormuz: a single attack on commercial shipping or energy infrastructure generates uncertainty, sharply increases insurance premiums, disrupts shipping patterns and imposes significant costs on global trade.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: The market should price recurring low-cost Iranian harassment rather than a binary closure scenario — war-risk insurance and freight rates are the transmission mechanism, not physical supply loss.
insights.quote: a single attack on commercial shipping, energy infrastructure or maritime traffic can generate uncertainty, sharply increase insurance premiums, disrupt shipping patterns and impose significant costs on global trade flows
insights.locator: Iran’s asymmetric strategy relies on its geographic advantage

insights.claim: Iran has founded the Persian Gulf Strait Association (PGSA), which seeks to institutionalise Tehran's control over the Strait of Hormuz by creating a formal mechanism for regulating maritime transit and collecting tolls from commercial vessels.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: A permanent Iranian toll regime on Hormuz would convert episodic risk into a structural cost on roughly a fifth of seaborne oil — the single most consequential development to track for energy logistics.

insights.claim: Tehran views control of the Strait of Hormuz not as a maritime advantage but as a lever on what it has long regarded as the region's 'soft underbelly' — the Gulf monarchies' dependence on energy exports, tourism, maritime trade and external security guarantees.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Iranian pressure will be aimed at Gulf economic diversification assets — tourism, logistics hubs, FDI flows — not just oil terminals.

insights.claim: Despite extensive military and economic damage, Tehran retained the four coercive capabilities that matter most to Gulf policymakers: threatening energy infrastructure, disrupting maritime trade, activating proxy networks and imposing recurring costs on neighbours.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Battle damage assessments understate residual Iranian capability; Gulf risk premia should not compress on reports of Iranian military losses.

themes.theme: Erosion of the American security umbrella

insights.claim: Operation Epic Fury demonstrated Washington's inability to fully shield its Gulf partners and their critical infrastructure from sustained Iranian attack, despite decades of American military predominance in the region.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: US security guarantees no longer suppress infrastructure risk in the Gulf — insurers and project financiers should price Gulf assets on their own vulnerability, not on the American umbrella.
insights.locator: Despite decades of American military predominance in the Gulf

insights.claim: Iran's September 2019 attacks on the Saudi Aramco facilities at Abqaiq and Khurais were the turning point in Gulf confidence, because Washington neither prevented the strike nor responded to it despite its extensive regional military presence.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: The Gulf's hedging behaviour has a seven-year track record with a clear origin point — this is a structural trend, not a reaction to the current administration.
insights.locator: Iran’s September 2019 attacks on the Saudi Aramco oil facilities

insights.claim: The Carter Doctrine of 1980, announced after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, established Washington as the external guarantor of Persian Gulf security — a 45-year framework the current conflict has now called into question.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: The end of the Carter Doctrine's credibility is a regime change in Middle East security architecture with multi-decade implications for defence procurement and energy routing.
insights.locator: Following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan

insights.claim: The Gulf monarchies' operating principle is that the United States remains their indispensable security partner but indispensability should not be confused with omnipotence.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: A compact model for Gulf behaviour: continued US arms purchases and basing coexist with independent accommodation of Iran — do not read one as contradicting the other.
insights.quote: while the United States remains the Gulf monarchies’ indispensable security partner, indispensability should not be confused with omnipotence
insights.locator: This shift reflected a broader strategic calculation

insights.claim: Delegations from nearly every Gulf state — Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and Kuwait — travelled to Tehran for the funeral of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killed in an Israeli airstrike, with the United Arab Emirates the notable exception in declining to send a senior delegation.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: The most visible signal yet that Gulf capitals will not align with Washington against Tehran — a constraint on any US coalition-building for further strikes.
insights.locator: Delegations from nearly every Gulf state

insights.claim: Gulf attendance at Khamenei's funeral reflected realpolitik rather than ideological affinity: Tehran remains an indispensable regional actor whose ability to shape the Gulf security environment cannot be ignored even after severe military damage.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Diplomatic gestures toward Iran should be read as risk management by exposed neighbours, not as a shift in alignment or sympathy.
insights.quote: Their participation reflected neither ideological affinity nor support for Iran’s regional policies.
insights.locator: Delegations from nearly every Gulf state

insights.claim: The Saudi-Iranian rapprochement brokered by China in March 2023 and the UAE's restoration of ambassador-level ties with Iran that same year were direct consequences of eroding confidence in the American security umbrella.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Chinese diplomatic capital in the Gulf grows directly out of perceived US unreliability — a structural transfer of influence that accelerates with each unanswered Iranian strike.
insights.locator: Rather than relying exclusively on Washington

insights.claim: Gulf leaders are refusing to choose between Washington and Beijing, confrontation and diplomacy, or deterrence and engagement, pursuing all simultaneously through a multi-aligned strategy that includes expanding indigenous defence capabilities and reducing dependence on any single power.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Expect continued Gulf capital and technology deals with Chinese counterparties despite US pressure — export-control and AI-chip restrictions on the Gulf will keep facing friction.
insights.quote: Rather than choosing between Washington and Beijing, confrontation and diplomacy, deterrence and engagement, Gulf leaders increasingly pursue all these simultaneously in a multi-aligned manner.
insights.locator: The result has been a more pronounced hedging strategy

insights.claim: The United Arab Emirates absorbed the largest share of Iranian missile and drone attacks and initially retaliated with direct strikes, then quickly recalibrated and covertly rebuilt economic and diplomatic ties with Tehran even as the ceasefire unravelled.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Even the most hawkish Gulf state reverts to accommodation within weeks — a strong prior that Gulf escalation is self-limiting and short-lived.
insights.quote: Yet Abu Dhabi quickly recalibrated its approach, recognising that continued confrontation with Tehran risked undermining its economic interests
insights.locator: Most indicative of this hedging approach

insights.claim: The UAE simultaneously deepened security ties with the United States and Israel while rebuilding relations with Iran, demonstrating that Gulf pragmatism does not require choosing a side.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Abraham Accords-style alignment and Iranian accommodation are not mutually exclusive — do not model Gulf policy as a binary.
insights.locator: This, despite Abu Dhabi deepening its security ties

insights.claim: Gulf national agendas, most notably Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030, depend on economic diversification, foreign direct investment in tourism, logistics and artificial intelligence, and continued hydrocarbon strength — all of which require a stable regional environment now threatened by prolonged conflict.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Sustained conflict directly threatens the FDI assumptions underpinning Gulf giga-projects and AI data-centre buildouts — watch for project deferrals as the tell.

insights.claim: In the weeks before the February outbreak of war, the Gulf states worked feverishly to de-escalate tensions with Iran, fearing the consequences of a sustained conflict for their development plans.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Gulf states act as a de-escalatory force ahead of conflict — their diplomatic activity is a useful leading indicator of imminent escalation.

insights.claim: Gulf policymakers judge the success of a war not by targets destroyed, commanders eliminated or missiles intercepted, but by whether the use of force produced a more stable and secure regional order.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: A transferable scorecard for reading Gulf reactions to Israeli or American operations — expect public coolness toward militarily successful campaigns that destabilise.
insights.quote: the ultimate measure of success is not the number of targets destroyed, commanders eliminated or missiles intercepted. Rather, it is whether the use of force produced a more stable and secure regional order
insights.locator: For Riyadh, Abu Dhabi, Doha and the other Gulf capitals

insights.claim: Modern conflicts increasingly reveal a widening gap between tactical success and lasting strategic change, as superior military performance does not automatically translate into favourable political outcomes.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Apply the same discount to headline military victories elsewhere — impressive strike footage is a poor predictor of durable political and market outcomes.
insights.quote: Modern conflicts increasingly reveal a widening gap between tactical success and their ability to bring about lasting strategic change
insights.locator: The broader lesson extends well beyond the Gulf

insights.claim: Israel and the United States showed unprecedented operational capabilities and inflicted significant damage on Iran's military infrastructure during Operation Epic Fury, making the campaign undeniably impressive on tactical and operational grounds.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: The authors concede the military case fully, which strengthens their strategic critique — the disappointment is not about capability but about outcome.
insights.locator: Much of the commentary following Operation Epic Fury

insights.claim: Iran emerged from Operation Epic Fury having absorbed significant damage yet with its coercive capabilities intact and its ability to dictate the terms of the regional order enhanced.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: A net-relative-gain read on Iran that runs against Western framings of the war — implies persistent, not diminishing, Middle East risk premia.
insights.quote: Iran absorbed significant military damage, but it maintained its coercive capabilities and enhanced its ability to shape and dictate the terms of the regional order

insights.claim: The Gulf monarchies ended the war facing exactly the same predicament they had before it: dependence on an external power that cannot fully guarantee their security while their critical infrastructure is attacked by Iran to no avail.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: No structural improvement in Gulf security means the risk premium embedded in Gulf energy and infrastructure assets should not normalise post-ceasefire.

insights.claim: The Gulf monarchies' objective is neither victory over Iran nor reconciliation with it, but the preservation of strategic autonomy in an increasingly uncertain international environment.
insights.speaker: Yoel Guzansky and Jesse R. Weinberg
insights.so_what: Strategic autonomy as the stated goal means Gulf sovereign wealth deployment will keep diversifying across US, Chinese and regional counterparties regardless of Washington's preferences.
